text: Hyperbaric oxy- gen therapy increases tissue oxygenation and has been used particularly in radiation-induced haemorrhagic cysti- tis to treat radionecrosis and tissue ischaemia.3,4 Cryosur- gery using liquid nitrogen has been used rarely.1 In cases that do not respond to drug treatment, surgical op- tions include urinary diversion, internal iliac artery embol- isation, unilateral hypogastric artery ligation, and if all else fails, cystectomy.1-3 Hydrodistension, the application of pressure to the bladder wall by an inflated balloon, has also been used.4 However, anaesthesia is required, its effect is short-lived, and it is associated with the risk of bladder per- foration.1,2,4 Prophylaxis to reduce the risk of haemorrhagic cystitis as- sociated with high-dose cyclophosphamide and ifosfa- mide includes intravenous hydration with diuresis, fre- quent voiding of the bladder or bladder catheterisation Urological Drugs 2179 The symbol † denotes a preparation no longer actively marketed The symbol  denotes a substance whose use may be restricted in certain sports (see p.vii) with sodium chloride 0.9% irrigation, and the use of mesna as a uroprotectant.1,2 Improvements in radiotherapy tech- niques are reducing the risk of radiation-induced haemor- rhagic cystitis.3 1. Interstitial cystitis is a chronic in- flammatory condition of the bladder that mainly affects middle-aged women.1-4 There are also rare reports of the condition occurring in children, usually girls.5 Symptoms include perineal and pelvic pain (that is often relieved by voiding), urinary frequency, urgency, and nocturia. Inter- stitial cystitis is a disease of unknown aetiology and sug- gested possible causes have included abnormal bladder epithelial permeability, neurogenic abnormalities, auto- immune disorders, and allergic reactions with increased mast-cell activation.1,2 It is considered to be incurable; at- tempts at management have included local and systemic drug therapy and surgery.
